extracted.intended_audience: students, merchants, and practitioners learning/proving arithmetic and proportional methods (historic/medieval Italian context)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural rules and worked examples for computing with proportions (binary, triple, quadruple), solving scale/weight, wage and trade problems, and methods such as single/double false position (regola delle due false posizioni). The text gives operational rules, identities, and worked examples for producing and manipulating proportional numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply proportional parts separately
rubrics_metrics.description: When numbers are given in proportional parts, to multiply them you multiply each part separately (i.e., multiply corresponding terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly instructs that when you have proportional parts (le parti proportionali) you should 'multiplicarai ciascuna' — multiply each term/pair separately and assemble the result; worked examples show multiplying the first by a factor, the second by the same factor, etc., to produce new proportional terms. Use this when scaling a proportional sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadruple-proportion identity (first·fourth = second·third)
rubrics_metrics.description: For four numbers in proportion the product of the first and fourth equals the product of the second and third (a·d = b·c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript states and uses this equality to reduce equations and to find unknown terms among four proportional numbers — e.g., 'la prima moltiplicata per la quarta fa iguale alla seconda per la terza'. Use it to solve for a missing term by cross-multiplication and to check proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate further proportional terms by multiplying/dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: You may obtain additional proportional parts by multiplying or dividing existing proportional terms (doubling, tripling, etc.) to extend the proportional sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show producing the third or fourth proportional by multiplying earlier terms (e.g., doubling the sum to find other parts), and by systematic procedures (multiplying successive parts or halving/doubling) to produce required proportional entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce equations by bringing all terms to one side and equating
rubrics_metrics.description: To solve proportional equations, bring terms together (reduce the equation), compare parts and reduce the equation to a form where you can read off the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly says to 'reducendo la equatione tutta a mano' and to equate parts after appropriate multiplications; this is the recommended algebraic-style reduction used in examples to isolate unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of single and double false position (regola delle due false posizioni / cataym)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve linear (and some compound) problems by making one or two trial (false) assumptions and combining/scaling their results to obtain the true value (single or double false position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called in the text 'regola Delle Doi falfe posizioni' and 'cataym', the method: make a trial guess, compute its consequence, then scale (or combine two trials) to reach the demanded true value. The manuscript explains both single and double false-position variants with examples and prescribes always giving the true name to the final result. Use when direct proportional setup is awkward or the problem is formulated in words (trade, wages, distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple (and higher) proportion methods
rubrics_metrics.description: There are operational rules for problems with triple or more proportional relationships (proporzione tripla, quadrupla), including how to combine and manipulate multiple proportional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author provides rules for composing triple proportions by repeated application of the binary proportion rules, and for managing multiple proportional sequences by multiplying/duplicating parts and keeping track of terms. Use the specified reductions and examples to handle chained proportional relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance/weights (scale) problem procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve scale/balance problems by placing and combining weights on both pans and using proportional reasoning to determine missing weights or equivalences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous worked examples show placing specified amounts on one side and other amounts on the other, then reasoning (often by combining standard units, doubling, or adding parts) until equilibrium. The text prescribes concrete manipulations of weights (putting sums together, moving portions from one side to another) to reach the asked balance; follow those stepwise compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-rate and wages proportional computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute distribution of wages, work-days, and related payments by proportional scaling between number of workers, days, and total pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a master finishing work in a given number of days, daily wages, how many workers or days correspond to given pay. The recommended approach is to set up proportional relations between persons and days, or to use doubling/halving to scale known cases to the wanted case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade, measure, and conversion calculations via proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute purchases, conversions of measures (weights, coins, legha/legha, canne, etc.), and profit–capital relations by setting proportional relations and scaling accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text walks through examples (buying flowers, converting legha to fiorini, capital and gain relations) demonstrating multiplication/division and proportional scaling to find unknown prices, totals, or change. Use the same proportional rules and the quadruple-proportion identity to convert between units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of systematic doubling/tripling (binary expansion) to produce sums
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing large sums or required counts, repeatedly double or triple known quantities (and sum selected doubles) to produce arbitrary totals (a practical decomposition strategy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript teaches producing sums by successive doubling (redoppiare) and adding selected doubles (e.g., produce 364 by chosen doublings and sums). This is recommended as a pragmatic device to assemble any demanded integer total from base parts; examples show explicit doubling tables and selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit multiplications to integral/feasible amounts; avoid overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying proportional constructions, avoid producing fractions or exceeding feasible integer bounds unless explicitly allowed — work in integral parts when possible and prefer decomposition methods that keep quantities integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions about not exceeding integer integrability 'ma nò piu' and about practicality (e.g., avoid producing more than the needed integer units), advising readers to adapt procedures to the available units and to use experienced judgment when composing parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer many worked examples and practice; verify by alternative reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn proportional methods by many concrete examples; verify results by alternate reductions or algebraic checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise emphasizes practicing with numerous examples, checking via reduction of equations and alternative constructions, and using algebraic verifications where possible. The text explicitly encourages repeated practice and cross-checks for certainty.
